targets.title: Criticizing groups from the inside and the outside: An identity perspective on the intergroup sensitivity effect
targets.evidence_quote: Serial mediation analyses confirmed past theorizing on the processes underlying the ISE (Hornsey & Imani, 2004;Thürmer & McCrea, 2018). Specifically, participants ascribed less constructive motives to outgroup commenters, leading to higher threat perceptions. Source and target effects on bonus payment were serially mediated by message motive and message threat ratings.

targets.title: Social identity and social convention in responses to criticisms of groups
targets.evidence_quote: Sutton et al. (2008) included such a comparison and found consistent evidence for both the classic ISE and the bystander ISE, with both effects being of similar magnitude.
targets.outcome_quote: In contrast, we observed a bystander ISE that was consistently and substantially larger than the classic ISE across all measures. Although more in line with a normative perspective, general norms against intergroup criticism would also not predict any effects of the target group's identity. Likewise, we observed significant main effects of target, such that individuals were more likely to deny a bonus to commenters who criticized an outgroup than to those who criticized the ingroup.

targets.authors: Thürmer, J. L., McCrea, S. M., & McIntyre, B. M.
targets.title: Motivated collective defensiveness: Group members prioritize counterarguing outgroup criticism over getting their work done
targets.evidence_quote: We conducted additional exploratory tests to determine whether identification with the ingroup could account for the observed results. In particular, it is possible we did not observe more support for the social identity account because participants were not sufficiently identified with the ingroup. We therefore examined whether the classic and bystander ISE effects were consistent across levels of identification. In line with previous research (Thürmer et al., 2019), Johnson-Neyman Analyses indicated that the behavioural classic ISE on participants' bonus payment decision was significant for those participants reporting medium-tohigh identification with their group (2.45 and above), but not for those reporting low identification (Figure 1a). 1 The bystander ISE was significant at all levels of identification (Figure 1b). Importantly, these analyses show that both the classic ISE and the bystander ISE are significant for individuals strongly identifying with the ingroup.
targets.outcome_quote: Further exploratory analysis also showed evidence for the role of identity, though not in line with the predictions of a social identity account. In line with past research, the classic behavioural ISE only emerged for those sufficiently identified with their group. In contrast, the behavioural bystander ISE was observed across levels of ingroup identification. We observed a parallel pattern of results for reported message threat, though not for message motive.
